#### Meta **Requires:** Python `>=3.10`
**Provides-Extra:** `numpy`, `cloudpickle`, `dev`, `docs`, `all`
[Package Info](package-info.html) ::: ``` ________ /\ \ / \ pymizu\ \ / 水 / \/_______/ ``` pymizu uses shared memory to make communication between Python processes fast enough to parallelize work at thread granularity. Task round trips drop from around 100 µs over sockets to under a microsecond — two orders of magnitude (see [Benchmarks](#benchmarks)). The hot path never enters the kernel and data is never copied through a system socket. In the default CPython build, the GIL runs CPU-bound threads on one core at a time, so compute parallelism in Python usually means multiple processes. Processes also isolate failures: a worker that crashes does not take the host down with it. Channels and work-stealing task pools run over POSIX shared memory (Linux, macOS) or Win32 file mappings (Windows): lock-free single-producer single-consumer rings with batched publication, spin-then-park waiting, and peer death delivered as an OS event. pymizu is built on [libmizu](https://github.com/shikokuchuo/libmizu), a C library for lock-free shared-memory IPC. [mizu](https://github.com/shikokuchuo/mizu) binds the same core for R, so Python and R can talk to each other. - Zero-copy numpy arrays and Arrow interchange (pyarrow, polars, pandas, duckdb) - Drop-in `concurrent.futures.Executor` — real `Future`s, `wait`, `as_completed`, `asyncio.wrap_future` - Event-driven asyncio — `await` tasks and maps, `async for` and `recv_async()` on channels — wake-ups as data arrives, no polling threads - Reproducible parallel random numbers (`seed=`) — identical results for any worker count or steal order - Nested parallel maps — a task can map over its own pool, deadlock-free > **Pre-release.** The API is not stable and may change at any time before a release. ### Installation ```sh pip install git+https://github.com/shikokuchuo/pymizu ``` Requires Python 3.10 or later on a 64-bit platform. See [Installation](user-guide/installation.qmd) for platform notes, optional extras, and deployment on Linux. ### Quickstart ::: {#8eff5952 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pymizu with pymizu.Pool.create(4) as pool: task = pool.submit(pow, 2, 16) result = task.collect(timeout=5) result ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 65536 ``` ::: ::: ### Benchmarks Communication overhead against the stdlib `concurrent.futures` pools (Apple M4 Pro, from `benchmarks/mizu-stdlib-bench.py`). Against `ProcessPoolExecutor` (tasks run in separate processes, with pickled payloads): | Benchmark | pymizu | ProcessPoolExecutor | Speedup | |----|----|----|----| | Trivial task round trip | 0.7 µs | 94.2 µs | 135x | | Pipelined throughput, 1 worker | 2,390,000 tasks/s | 18,500 tasks/s | 129x | | Parallel map overhead, trivial function, 4 workers | 0.4 µs/elt* | 70.3 µs/elt | 176x | | Parallel map of 2,000 ~5 µs tasks, 4 workers | 4.3 ms | 129 ms | 30x | Against `ThreadPoolExecutor` (tasks share one process, so the GIL caps CPU-bound work at a single core): | Benchmark | pymizu | ThreadPoolExecutor | Speedup | |----|----|----|----| | Trivial task round trip | 0.7 µs | 9.5 µs | 14x | | Pipelined throughput, 1 worker | 2,390,000 tasks/s | 405,000 tasks/s | 5.9x | | Parallel map overhead, trivial function, 4 workers | 0.4 µs/elt* | 2.6 µs/elt | 6.5x | | Parallel map of 2,000 ~5 µs tasks, 4 workers | 4.3 ms | 50 ms | 12x | \* elt = element; microseconds of wall time per map element. See [Benchmarks](user-guide/benchmarks.qmd) for how pymizu compares with other frameworks, and for the benchmark scripts. ### Drop-in `concurrent.futures` `PoolExecutor` adapts a pool to the stdlib `concurrent.futures.Executor` interface — code written against `ProcessPoolExecutor` drops in, and `submit` returns real `Future` objects: ::: {#0752a0f0 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} with pymizu.PoolExecutor.create(4) as ex: futures = [ex.submit(pow, 2, i) for i in range(4)] result = [f.result() for f in futures] result ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [1, 2, 4, 8] ``` ::: ::: See [Task pools](user-guide/pools.qmd#concurrentfutures-interop) for wrapping an existing pool and how cancellation works. ### Parallel map `Pool.map(fn, x)` maps `fn` over `x` on the pool and returns the run's handle immediately. The function and data cross into shared memory once. Workers divide the elements among themselves. `handle.collect()` returns the results in order — or `await handle` in asyncio code. A map also nests — the mapped function can map over its own pool with `pymizu.current_pool()`, deadlock-free. ::: {#0f4d0063 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} with pymizu.Pool.create(4) as pool: result = pool.map(abs, range(-5, 5)).collect() result ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4] ``` ::: ::: See [Parallel map](user-guide/map.qmd). ### R interop Pool workers can be R processes that run the [mizu](https://github.com/shikokuchuo/mizu) package, the R binding of the same core. `pymizu.r_launcher()` spawns them and `pymizu.call()` describes the task — here R's built-in `mtcars` summarized by R itself, read back into polars: ```python import polars as pl import pymizu with pymizu.Pool.create(4, launcher=pymizu.r_launcher()) as pool: task = pool.submit( pymizu.call(source="aggregate(mpg ~ cyl, data = mtcars, FUN = mean)") ) print(pl.DataFrame(task.collect())) ``` - A numpy array arrives in R as a numeric vector, and a polars, pyarrow, or pandas frame as a data frame - A vector or data frame arrives back as a numpy array or a `pymizu.Frame` - Arrow data (pyarrow tables and record batch readers, or any `__arrow_c_stream__` producer) crosses the same way The mizu README shows the reverse direction: an R host that drives Python workers with `mizu_py_pool_launcher()`. See [R interop](user-guide/interop.qmd). ### Where next - [Benchmarks](user-guide/benchmarks.qmd) — overhead against the stdlib pools, and how pymizu compares with other frameworks. - [Channels](user-guide/channels.qmd) — sending and receiving, batch operations, and what crosses a channel. - [Task pools](user-guide/pools.qmd) — outcomes, nested tasks, growing and observing a pool. - [Parallel map](user-guide/map.qmd) — scheduling, reproducible randomness, templates, prepared maps. - [R interop](user-guide/interop.qmd) — R peers and workers, what crosses the language boundary, and the dtype matrix. - [API reference](reference/index.qmd) — the generated function and class reference.
